analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal facial recognition and biometric surveillance unless Congress explicitly authorizes it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; its only action in two years was referral to two House committees on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for any federal agency, employee, or contractor to buy, hold, or use facial recognition or other remote biometric identification tools — face, voice, or gait — in the United States unless Congress later passes a law spelling out exactly who could use such a tool, for what purpose, and under what accuracy, privacy, and due-process safeguards [S2] [S3]. Evidence gathered unlawfully could not be used by the federal government in court, and individuals could sue for damages [S2] [S3]. It would also cut off federal Byrne public-safety grants to state and local governments that use biometric surveillance without a comparable ban of their own [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who would otherwise be scanned, identified, and tracked by government facial recognition systems in public spaces, at airports, and at the border, without ever consenting or knowing it happened. People misidentified by the technology would gain a right to sue for damages.

how_it_helps.text: No federal agency or official — including contractors — could acquire, possess, access, or use any biometric surveillance system, or data derived from one, unless Congress passes a specific act authorizing that use with named entities, purposes, accuracy standards, and privacy protections [S2] [S3].

Information obtained in violation of the ban could not be used by the federal government in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding, and anyone aggrieved by a violation could sue for actual damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees; state attorneys general could also sue on residents' behalf [S2] [S3].
State and local governments would lose Byrne grant law-enforcement funding unless they adopted substantially similar restrictions, extending the moratorium beyond federal agencies [S2] [S3].
The ban covers face, voice, and gait recognition everywhere inside U.S. borders, including airports, ports of entry, and border zones [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies and their technology vendors would lose access to facial recognition and voice-identification tools currently in use, and state and local police departments that keep using the technology would forfeit Byrne grant money.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a blanket moratorium, not an accuracy standard: it bars all government use of facial recognition and voice identification until Congress affirmatively legislates, which would also foreclose uses its critics consider legitimate, such as identifying criminal suspects, missing children, or unconscious patients [S2] [S3].

Conditioning Byrne grants on adopting a state-level ban ties federal public-safety money to a specific privacy policy, which states that want to keep the technology for policing would experience as a funding penalty [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: government facial recognition can help solve crimes and find missing people, but it also lets the government identify and track anyone who walks down a public street, with documented accuracy problems across demographic groups in commercial systems. This bill resolves that trade decisively toward privacy — a ban first, with a narrow, demanding path for Congress to authorize specific uses later. Reasonable people can argue the moratorium is too blunt, but the bill does not hide that choice; it makes authorization deliberately hard, which is the point.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Oversight Committees the day it was introduced in March 2023, and neither committee ever took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 7, 2023, with 10 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and to the Committee on Oversight and Accountability [S5].
That referral was the bill's last recorded action; no hearing, markup, or vote followed in the two years remaining in the Congress [S5].
Support stayed at 15 House members, all Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and surveillance technology vendors keep using and selling facial recognition with no new statutory limits, and police departments keep Byrne grant money without adopting restrictions; nobody gained protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Surveillance vendors and agencies keep the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican ever signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill had no committee champion and was never taken up [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance technology vendors
industries.note: The bill would close off the government market for face, voice, and gait recognition products — the bill bars federal agencies from buying the systems and cuts Byrne grants to state and local buyers. Its interest in keeping that market open runs against the privacy of the people being scanned [S3].

industries.industry: Federal and state law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would lose an investigative tool they currently use without statutory limits, and state and local departments would face forfeiture of Byrne public-safety grants unless they adopt equivalent bans [S2] [S3].
